headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: gpt-engineer writes project files and can execute generated code, while airflow has broad network egress and may consume untrusted outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can write files in the project directory and B reads/writes that same workspace by default, so attacker-controlled content from A can be treated as instructions by B. Airflow itself has no browser or MCP bridge, but the shared filesystem plus B's file-driven workflow creates a plausible injection path.
conditions: IF agent_a writes prompt-like text into files that agent_b later ingests
IF both agents operate in the same project directory without content provenance checks
mitigations: Add a manual review step before B reads any file from A
Use separate project directories for the two agents
Prefix A-generated files as data-only and reject instruction-like tokens
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: B can read and write the project directory and has broad network egress, while A also has broad network egress and no stated data-class restrictions. Even though A touches no explicit sensitive class, the shared workspace means generated code or artifacts can be exposed externally by either agent.
conditions: IF sensitive material is placed in the shared project directory
IF either agent transmits file contents or derived artifacts to configured model APIs or external services
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared project directory
Use a local-only model endpoint for B
Restrict outbound network access during file review
Rotate any credentials stored in the workspace
requires-engineering: isolate per-agent storage and egress policies

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B has write_filesystem and per-project shared state, while A can also influence the same project artifacts through its API-driven workflow. Airflow does not advertise write_filesystem, so the conflict is asymmetric, but overlapping mutation of shared project files can still cause lost updates or inconsistent outputs.
conditions: IF both agents modify files in the same project directory
IF B runs multiple instances against the same project without external locking
mitigations: Run only one agent per project directory
Serialize edits with a simple lock file
Review diffs before accepting A's generated artifacts
Disable concurrent B sessions on the same workspace
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: B's workflow writes files and can execute generated code with the user's privileges, so if it treats A's outputs as authoritative, A's mistakes can cascade into code execution or committed project changes. Airflow's broad network egress increases the blast radius if downstream actions are triggered from bad artifacts.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated files or text as the basis for code execution
IF the generated code is run with the user's privileges
mitigations: Require human approval before executing any generated code
Inspect A's outputs for factual claims before B consumes them
Run B in a disposable sandbox for first execution
Limit network access during execution
requires-engineering: add automated verification of A's outputs

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent, so compliance risk is limited to generic workspace handling. Because A is source-available and B is open-source, there is no evidence here of a specific cross-border or regulated-data violation; the other agent is not cited beyond the shared workspace context.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared project directory
IF the deployment environment imposes residency or retention rules not reflected in either profile
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in the workspace
Document retention and deletion procedures
Use separate environments for regulated projects
requires-engineering: add policy checks before file writes
